The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center (“Ohio State”) is a public, academic health center that provides care to a high volume of Medicare and Medicaid patients. In 2024, around 71% of the patients served in our University Hospitals were covered by government programs or self-pay, including Medicare (34.6%) and Medicaid only (26.8%). Our service area is the entire state of Ohio, with more than 50% of our inpatient admissions being patients from Columbus and Franklin County, 16% coming from adjacent counties and 32% coming from other counties in Ohio outside of central Ohio.

Ohio State operates highly specialized health care programs that are essential to our community but are not always financially self-sustaining. Many of these services including our trauma, transplant, inpatient detoxification, outpatient behavioral health, and high-risk obstetrics programs care for a disproportionate share of patients who are uninsured or covered by Medicare and Medicaid.  Reimbursement of these services often falls short of the costs to provide care. 

Ohio State's Emergency Department operates around the clock as a regional trauma center, serving patients of all acuity levels, regardless of ability to pay. Federal law guarantees access to patients but does not guarantee adequate reimbursement for those providers. 340B savings help sustain the staffing and infrastructure needed to deliver that care safely.  

Other essential programs, such as Ohio State’s Labor & Delivery unit, receive high-risk referrals from hospitals across the region that lack the specialty capacity to safely manage complex pregnancies. Ohio State serves a significant share of Medicaid-covered mothers, and reimbursement consistently falls short of the costs of care. 340B savings help close that gap.

Ohio's behavioral health crisis is acute, and Ohio State is among the state's largest providers of inpatient and outpatient psychiatric care. Ohio State serves patients with severe mental illness, substance use disorders, and acute psychiatric crises.  Many of these patients are uninsured or covered by Medicaid at rates below the cost of care. 340B savings help sustain the staffing and services that keep these programs open and accessible.

Ohio State’s Medication Access Team ensures patients can obtain and afford the medications their providers prescribe. By removing insurance, financial, and administrative barriers, the team secures prior authorization approvals and connects patients to manufacturer assistance programs, grants, copay support, vouchers, and the Ohio State Medication Repository Program. Working directly with patients, providers, payers, and manufacturers, Medication Access Specialists navigate complex access requirements to prevent delays in treatment, reduce medication abandonment, and ensure equitable access to life-saving and life-changing therapies. Care coordination, medication assistance, and patient navigation are essential for helping patients navigate a complex healthcare system.  However, these services aren't reimbursed through traditional payment structures. 340B savings allow Ohio State to provide these services directly to patients, reducing patients' out-of-pocket costs and ensuring treatment is delivered as seamlessly as possible.

340B savings are reinvested in clinical operations that determine which services are available and at what capacity. At Ohio State, this translates into measurable impacts on access and care delivery across several dimensions.  340B savings support staffing levels and service capacity, enabling Ohio State to operate programs such as behavioral health, high-risk obstetrics, and trauma-level emergency care at volumes that Medicaid and Medicare reimbursement alone would not sustain. For patients who depend on these services, the practical outcome is access to care that would otherwise require traveling to another region or going without. 340B program savings help support many essential functions that are underfunded by Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal and state level funding programs for research and teaching.
